intro: Two runs of the aircraft as built, gear up and doors shut, at 100 m/s (Mach 0.29): at no angle of attack, and at 8 degrees, started from the first. Two angles are enough for what decides how it flies: how fast lift grows with angle, whether the nose-up moment grows with it (which is what unstable means), and the drag.
caption: At 8 degrees. The canards' and the wing's leading edges carry the deepest suction; the capped intakes and nozzles are the orange faces.
cd0_note: part of it is the blunt base of the capped nozzles, as on any powered-off model
notes: Unstable, and a little more so

The pitching moment rises with lift: a static margin of -6.8 % of the chord, against the -4.8 % our vortex-lattice code gave. That code sees only the lifting surfaces; the fuselage ahead of the CG adds its own nose-up moment, the usual difference. More instability asks more of the flight control computers.
Lift grows at 2.98 per radian, 4 % above the vortex-lattice figure: the canard and wing were modelled right, and the instantaneous turn rate, which lift sets, stands.

Drag is higher on both counts: 0.0222 at zero lift, and 28 % more drag due to lift than the assumed Oswald factor gives. Through the same energy-manoeuvrability sums the best sustained turn at sea level falls from 25.5 to 22.3 degrees a second.
